extracted.intended_audience: reporters, editors and newsroom staff at The Washington Post
extracted.subtask_description: Organizational policies and standards governing ethical conduct, sourcing, fact-checking, corrections, and newsroom behavior for Washington Post journalists and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest — gifts, travel and payments
rubrics_metrics.description: This news organization is pledged to avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance of conflict of interest wherever and whenever possible. We pay our own way. We accept no gifts from news sources. We accept no free trips. We neither seek nor accept preferential treatment that might be rendered because of the positions we hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions to the no-gift rule are few and obvious — invitations to meals, for example, may be accepted when they are occasional and innocent but not when they are repeated and their purpose is deliberately calculating. Free admissions to any event that is not free to the public are prohibited, with narrow exceptions (e.g., press box seats or tickets provided for a critic’s review) and whenever possible arrangements will be made to pay for such seats. We do not accept payment — either honoraria or expenses — from governments, government-funded organizations, groups of government officials, political groups or organizations that take positions on controversial issues. A reporter or editor also cannot accept payment from any person, company or organization that he or she covers. Be wary of disguised gratuities; avoid money from individuals, companies, trade associations or organizations that lobby government or try to influence issues the newspaper covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of partisan causes and public activism
rubrics_metrics.description: We avoid active involvement in any partisan causes — politics, community affairs, social action, demonstrations — that could compromise or seem to compromise our ability to report and edit fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private behavior as well as professional behavior must not bring discredit to the profession or The Post. Relatives' employment or involvement in causes should be disclosed to department heads because their ties can appear to compromise integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors of The Post are committed to fairness. Fairness results from a few simple practices: No story is fair if it omits facts of major importance or significance. Fairness includes completeness. No story is fair if it includes essentially irrelevant information at the expense of significant facts. Fairness includes relevance. No story is fair if it consciously or unconsciously misleads or even deceives the reader. Fairness includes honesty. No story is fair if it covers individuals or organizations that have not been given the opportunity to address assertions or claims about them made by others. Fairness includes diligently seeking comment and taking that comment genuinely into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek comment from those the story concerns and take it genuinely into account. Avoid omitting significant facts or inserting irrelevant material that distracts from key information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post respects taste and decency, understanding that society’s concepts of taste and decency are constantly changing. We shall avoid prurience. We shall avoid profanities and obscenities unless their use is so essential to a story of significance that its meaning is lost without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscenities must have executive or managing editor approval. If content contains potentially offensive material with legitimate news value, use visual and/or text warnings (for example: 'Warning: Some images on this site contain graphic images of war'). Do not link to sites that aid or abet illegal activity; consult Legal if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of news and opinion; labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of news columns from the editorial pages is solemn and complete. This separation is intended to serve the reader, who is entitled to the facts in the news columns and to opinions on the editorial and 'op-ed' pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels: Analysis — interpretation of the news based on evidence; Perspective — discussion with a point of view or narrative by individuals; Opinion — a column or blog in the Opinions section; Review — a professional critic’s assessment. Opinion and analysis/commentary in news must be plainly labeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When using networks such as Facebook, Twitter, etc., for reporting or for our personal lives, we must protect our professional integrity and remember: Washington Post journalists are always Washington Post journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media accounts reflect on the newsroom; every comment or link should be considered public information regardless of privacy settings. Post journalists must refrain from writing, tweeting or posting anything — including photographs or video — that could objectively be perceived as reflecting political, racial, sexist, religious or other bias or favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the national and community interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post is vitally concerned with the national interest and with the community interest. The claim of national interest by a federal official does not automatically equate with the national interest. The claim of community interest by a local official does not automatically equate with the community interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serve the widest possible dissemination of information and evaluate claims of 'national' or 'community' interest rather than accepting them at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist role and identity — no misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should make every effort to remain in the audience, to be the stagehand rather than the star, to report the news, not to make the news. In gathering news, journalists will not misrepresent their identity or their occupation. They will not portray themselves as police officers, physicians or anything other than journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting should be honorable; be prepared to explain publicly any actions taken to get a story. Do not deceive sources about who you are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and fact-checking standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington Post reporters have primary responsibility for reporting, writing and fact-checking their stories. Stories are subject to review by one or more editors. The Post has a multilevel structure for the review and editing of stories that may include fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review may include assignment editors, multiplatform/copy editors and senior editors; the number of editors and extent of involvement varies with complexity, sensitivity and time pressure. Editors overseeing digital platforms may also be involved in presentation, headlines, news alerts and newsletters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post strives for a nimble, accurate and complete news report. We endeavor to be promptly responsive in correcting errors in material published on digital platforms and in print. When we run a correction, clarification or editor’s note, our goal is to tell readers, as clearly and quickly as possible, what was wrong and what is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a correction, clarification or editor’s note whenever a significant mistake is corrected. Clarifications are for language that is correct but unclear or when we initially failed to seek comment. Editor’s notes are for corrections that call into question the entire substance of an article or raise significant ethical matters and require senior-editor approval. When readers find errors in comments, indicate in comments that it has been corrected. Correct alerts and social network errors on the platform where they occurred. Do not attribute blame to individual reporters or editors in correction language (e.g., avoid 'because of a reporting error').

rubrics_metrics.name: Take-down (unpublish) requests
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of editorial policy, we do not grant take-down requests, which should be vetted at the highest level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject claims inaccuracy, investigate and, if necessary, publish a correction rather than removing the article. Consider further editorial action (updates, follow-ups) as warranted. Take-down requests for publicly available personal data will be reviewed if the person involved is under threat of physical harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on sources and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post is committed to disclosing to its readers the sources of the information in its stories to the maximum possible extent. Named sources are vastly to be preferred to unnamed sources. Reporters should press to have sources go on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be reluctant to grant anonymity; editors have an obligation to know the identity of unnamed sources used in a story. Prefer at least two independent sources for factual information that depends on confidential informants; prefer firsthand/direct knowledge or a relevant document as a second source. Publish from a single source only after deliberations involving the executive editor, managing editor and department head, depending on reliability. Strive to tell readers why unnamed sources deserve confidence and avoid vague attributions like 'sources' or 'informed sources.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground rules and attribution categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Start virtually all interviews with the presumption that they are on the record. The Post defines: On the record — attributable by name; On background / not for attribution — attributable in a limited way (e.g., 'a police department official'); Deep background — information included but not attributed; Off the record — information not to be used for publication or further reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain and agree ground rules before interviews, preferably on tape. Avoid deep background where possible because it prevents readers from understanding the source. Be extremely careful about 'off the record' and clarify differences; if a source insists on secrecy to editors, resist and treat information as unusable. If unsure about terms, discuss with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with sources — fairness, context and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: We strive to treat sources fairly. This means putting statements we quote into context, and summarizing the arguments of people we quote in ways that are recognizably fair and accurate. Potentially controversial statements by public figures and others should be quoted in a complete sentence or paragraph when possible, and in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking comment, give subjects a reasonable opportunity to respond; do not call at the last minute if avoidable. Do not promise sources that we will refrain from additional reporting. Do not publish ad hominem quotations from unnamed sources or blind quotations whose only purpose is color. We do not use pseudonyms and do not mislead readers about identities; decisions to use less than a full name require editor participation and explanation to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: We must be truthful about the source of our information. Facts and quotations in a story that were not produced by our own reporting must be attributed. Attribution of material from other media must be total. Readers should be able to distinguish between what the reporter saw and what the reporter obtained from other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a premium on original reporting and, when reporter was not present at a scene, make that clear. Assertions about events unseen by the reporter should be attributed. If reconstructing statements or exchanges based on recollections, attribute transparently. Discuss with editors when special attribution problems arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting sources and sharing drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Our objective in quoting people is to capture both their words and intended meaning accurately. We do not allow sources to change the rules governing specific quotations after the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a source asks to read quotations back, do not allow them to change the original quote; permitting a source to add to a quotation and then explaining that sequence to readers is preferable. Sharing sections of stories with sources for technical accuracy is acceptable, but sharing entire drafts of stories with outside sources prior to publication is against policy except in extremely rare circumstances with executive or managing editor permission. Be prepared that communications with sources may become public; make no promises incompatible with policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert sources and sourcing diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: We quote many people and depend on experts to provide context, interpretation and judgments. We must strive always to get a rich variety of voices into our work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dependence on the same academics or public figures; seek new specialists including women, younger people, people of color, unconventional thinkers and those not routinely quoted. Include voices of ordinary citizens affected by events (students, teachers, employees, etc.). Make an active effort to expand the universe of sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity is at the core of Washington Post journalism. Accurately reporting stories from the United States and around the world means engaging a variety of voices as interviewees and first-person writers, striving for a staff that reflects a range of backgrounds and life experiences, and seeking feedback from all who would give it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post releases an annual report on staff diversity and actively pursues inclusion in sourcing and staffing decisions.
